title: The Third Declension — Consonant Stems
subtitle: ὁ φύλαξ, ὁ γέρων, ἡ ἐλπίς — the nominative disguises the stem.
objectives: Decline third-declension consonant-stem nouns in all five cases and both numbers.
Understand that the genitive singular reveals the true stem.
Recognize the patterns: labial stems (π, β, φ), velar stems (κ, γ, χ), dental stems (τ, δ, θ), nasal stems (ν), liquid stems (ρ), sibilant stems (σ).

sections.heading: The third declension
sections.body:
The third declension contains nouns of all three genders. The stems end in consonants or vowels. The nominative singular is often disguised by sound changes; the genitive singular shows the true stem.

φύλαξ (guard) has the stem φυλακ-. The nominative singular drops the κ and shows only φύλαξ. The genitive singular is φύλακος, revealing the stem.

The third declension is more varied than the first and second. You must learn the genitive singular for every third-declension noun, because the nominative alone does not tell you the stem.

sections.heading: Velar stems: ὁ φύλαξ (guard)
sections.body:
Stem: φυλακ- (the κ drops before σ in the nominative)
              singular        plural
  nominative  φύλαξ           φύλακες
  genitive    φύλακος         φυλάκων
  dative      φύλακι          φύλαξι(ν)
  accusative  φύλακα          φύλακας
  vocative    φύλαξ           φύλακες

The dative plural φύλαξι comes from φυλακ-σι: the κ + σ produces ξ.

sections.heading: Dental stems: ἡ ἐλπίς (hope)
sections.body:
Stem: ἐλπιδ- (the δ drops before σ in the nominative)
              singular        plural
  nominative  ἐλπίς           ἐλπίδες
  genitive    ἐλπίδος         ἐλπίδων
  dative      ἐλπίδι          ἐλπίσι(ν)
  accusative  ἐλπίδα          ἐλπίδας
  vocative    ἐλπίς           ἐλπίδες

The dative plural ἐλπίσι comes from ἐλπιδ-σι: the δ drops before σ.

sections.heading: Nasal stems: ὁ γέρων (old man)
sections.body:
Stem: γεροντ- (the τ drops in the nominative)
              singular        plural
  nominative  γέρων           γέροντες
  genitive    γέροντος        γερόντων
  dative      γέροντι         γέρουσι(ν)
  accusative  γέροντα         γέροντας
  vocative    γέρον           γέροντες

The dative plural γέρουσι is irregular (from an older form).

items.prompt: What case reveals the true stem of a third-declension noun?
Why is the nominative singular often disguised?
items.answer: Because final consonants drop or change according to sound laws.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 3.8 introduces the third declension vowel and σ-stems: ἡ πόλις (city), ὁ βασιλεύς (king), τὸ γένος (race). These stems end in vowels or sigma, and they show compensatory lengthening and contraction patterns.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark the lesson complete when you can decline φύλαξ, ἐλπίς, and γέρων from memory and can identify the stem of any third-declension noun from its genitive singular.
